chapter_theme: Gandharvadattai's song falters and she loses the vina contest, garlands Civakan and is screened from the hall; Kattiyankaran, burning with envy, taunts the defeated suitors into attacking Civakan for the bride, and Civakan's friend Padumukan sees through him, tells the kings that force after a lost contest disgraces them and that the chosen bride is beyond their reach, exposes the usurper's plan to let them destroy one another, and shoots an arrow through stone.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, known here as the merchant Kantukkan's son
daughter of the Vidyadhara king, defeated by Civakan at the vina
the crowd watching the vina contest
the minister who seized Saccandan's throne, called the guardian king here
kings who came seeking the princess and lost to her at the vina
Civakan's friend and companion, who answers the kings

733.reading: In her song Gandharvadattai asks a woman with eyes like a stained spear whether her lover does not see that her crescent brow, wide eyes and full breasts are drowned in pallor, while lightning flashes over the long hill with its silver falls.
733.event: Gandharvadattai sings the second stanza of her song in the vina contest.
733.nuance: The stanza repeats the frame of 732 with the refrain காணார்கொல் கேள்வர்: an akam song of a woman pale in separation, sung by a princess who is herself waiting to learn whom she must marry. The addressee is the song's heroine, not anyone in the hall.

734.reading: The next stanza asks the woman of sugarcane-sweet speech the same question: does her lover not see her rare breasts, bamboo-soft shoulders and fine crescent brow drowned in red pallor, while lightning flashes over the long hill of crowded gem-bright falls?
734.event: Gandharvadattai sings the third stanza of her song.
734.nuance: Three stanzas (732 to 734) vary only the epithets, as in a vari song; the lightning on the hill is the season sign that the absent lover should have returned by.

735.reading: Her tune goes one way and her song another, the soft fingers of her bangled hand no longer move on the bright string, her throat trembles, and the woman sits defeated at music beyond reckoning.
735.event: Gandharvadattai's playing and singing fall apart, and she loses the contest to Civakan.
735.nuance: The defeat is told as a body failing at its art (tune, song, finger and throat parting from one another), not as a judgment by referees. எண்ணின்றி (line 4) may mean 'past counting' or 'without her wits'.

736.reading: Broken at her great jewelled harp, wasting, trembling and overcome with shame, the kohl-eyed princess, as if lifting a mountain, raises the golden garland for the man of the flowered anklet.
736.event: Gandharvadattai, defeated, lifts the bridal garland for Civakan.
736.nuance: The garland weighs like a mountain: the shame of losing and the shyness of choosing are one weight, and the verse lets the reader feel both in the same gesture.

737.reading: With her anklets crying and her girdle flashing she steps softly, shy as a fine hen-swan, and drops the garland on the lord as if telling all the people of the world to make haste and perform high austerity.
737.event: Gandharvadattai lets the garland fall on Civakan.

claims.claim: such a union is the fruit of austerity, so all should hasten to perform it

737.nuance: The claim is the poet's fancy (என்பாள்போல், 'as if she said'), but it is the narrator's own: a bridal joy is presented as the reward of tapas done before. The verse names no school, though a Jain epic that ends in Civakan's renunciation here turns tapas toward the very pleasures it will later renounce.

738.reading: She fastens the golden garland on his chest like lightning born of a cloud falling on a gem mountain, bows at the young man's feet in worship and stands like the lotus goddess who shows the way of enjoyment, joined to him.
738.event: Gandharvadattai garlands Civakan and bows at his feet.

739.reading: Gazing at her red-flower feet, her hips, her breasts and her moon face, Civakan is struck with wonder, as if he would swallow her, and says the lady of the wide dark-flower eyes is the lotus goddess herself.
739.event: Civakan gazes at his bride and exclaims that she is the lotus goddess.
739.nuance: Her gaze went down to his feet (738); his travels over her from feet to face. மரைமலர்த் தேவி picks up the lotus goddess of 738 and is taken up in Kattiyankaran's திருமகள் (744), where the goddess of beauty becomes the goddess of sovereignty.

740.reading: As her garland and ear-jewels flash and her earrings throw out a rainbow, the girl bends in shyness like lightning in rain-cloud, and her loving companions lower the mechanical silk screen over her without mishap.
740.event: Gandharvadattai's companions lower a mechanical curtain to hide her.
740.nuance: எந்திர எழினி: the screen is a machine, like the peacock car of the earlier books; the princess is removed from the hall at the moment the kings' anger is about to break.

741.reading: When the crowd roared like the full-moon sea that Civakan, a man of radiance, had won the vina from the spear-eyed girl, the guardian king, burning within, spoke to all the kings.
741.event: The crowd hails Civakan's victory, and Kattiyankaran, burning with envy, addresses the assembled kings.
741.nuance: Kattiyankaran is called only காவல் மன்னன், the guardian king: the usurper holds the title of the protector. Line 3 (கள்ளராற் புலியை ஏறு காணிய) is obscure; it may compare him to a bull that sees a tiger brought on by thieves, or allude to the cattle raid of the earlier book, and the reading here does not rest on it.

742.reading: Kattiyankaran tells the kings that they have stained their lineage, lofty as the northern mountain, and are like fireflies before the rayed sun; if they fear the sword battle where men die, the scar of blame will last for ever, so let them give up their crowns and go into the hermits' forest.
742.event: Kattiyankaran taunts the defeated suitors as cowards fit only for the hermit forest.

claims.claim: a king who shrinks from battle should give up his crown and leave for the forest of ascetics

742.nuance: Renunciation is used here as an insult: to enter the முனிவனம் is the fate of a shamed king. The speaker means to provoke a fight he will not join, which 755 exposes, so the claim is the villain's and the work does not endorse it.

743.reading: He goes on: they who made of the jasmine ball of a girl a flowered hill fenced by three-musth elephants, whose broad chests bear saffron-smeared garlands, should wrap themselves in the cloak of fame, for tomorrow the goddess of fortune too will go to him.
743.event: Kattiyankaran warns the kings that royal fortune will follow the bride to the winner.
743.nuance: The lines as printed are out of order: line 2 ends with என்றான், and lines 3 and 4 read as the verse's opening, so the sense is taken in the order 3, 4, 1, 2. The image of the jasmine ball and the elephant-fenced hill is hard and may instead mock the kings' display; 'cloak of fame' reads as sarcasm.

744.reading: The man who has joined this goddess of fortune, he says, will become lord of the earth-woman clad in the clear sea and of the golden wheel of rule; if they defeat him on the battlefield, fortune is theirs; so spoke Kattiyankaran of black heart and poisoned, cruel words.
744.event: Kattiyankaran urges the kings to win sovereignty by killing Civakan.
744.nuance: The incitement is a lie that tells the truth: Civakan is the heir of the throne Kattiyankaran holds, and will indeed become lord of the earth. The narrator brands the speaker in line 4 (கருமன நச்சு வெஞ்சொல்), so the reader is not to take his promise to the kings as meant.

745.reading: He mocks them further: let them not falter in sullen thought that the frail-waisted girl, who cries 'mother!' in fear at the touch of an anicham garland, is one and they are many; they who have won only by stirring a lone pond with water squirted from jewelled syringes should go and take the lady.
745.event: Kattiyankaran goads the kings to seize the bride.
745.nuance: The verse seems to set the girl's softness against the kings' play-battles of the bathing pond, so that seizing her is made to look easy and their hesitation unmanly; the construction of lines 1 to 2 is unclear, and whose fear அம்மனையோ voices is not certain.

746.reading: At the fierce man's words the kings, roaring in haste and wanting the enjoyment of the unsagged breasts of the ball-playing girl, set out to plunge into the blazing fire of the anger of Kantukkan's son, strong-shouldered as a pillar, a five-headed serpent.
746.event: The suitor kings rise in uproar to fight Civakan for the bride.
746.nuance: The motive the narrator gives is lust (படாமுலைப் போகம் வேண்டி), not honour, though Kattiyankaran's taunts were all of honour. Civakan is still known only as the merchant Kantukkan's son.

747.reading: Padumukan, on his trained elephant amid his sea of troops, grasped what the unlearned Kattiyankaran had in mind, and as the kings rose to fight he spoke words at once cool, slight and burning.
747.event: Padumukan, Civakan's friend, sees through Kattiyankaran's scheme and begins to answer the kings.
747.nuance: கல்லாக் கட்டியங்காரன், 'Kattiyankaran who has no learning', is set against the contest just won by learning and against Padumukan's closing boast இற்று எமர் கல்வி (756).

748.reading: Padumukan says: to argue 'we lost to her at music, so we will win by elephants' is not fitting, and he says so pleading; it is a disgrace to every king to break the way that has come down by rule; let them go quickly to their own quarters, for fire burns when it is touched.
748.event: Padumukan tells the kings that taking the bride by force after losing the contest disgraces them, and bids them leave.

claims.claim: kings who lose a contest held by the agreed rule disgrace themselves if they seek the prize by force

748.nuance: இவட்குத் தோற்றாம் quotes the kings' own position: they had all been beaten by Gandharvadattai before Civakan beat her. The closing proverb makes the hidden prince the fire.

749.reading: Those who craved the nectar of her coral lips, won by the embrace of shoulders, would take it by the sword: long live their arts! Did they get the creeper-like daughter of the lion-like king? Let them grow light of foot and leap away over the earth.
749.event: Padumukan mocks the kings and tells them to flee.

claims.claim: a woman's love, which is won by embrace, cannot be taken by the sword

749.nuance: வாழ்க நுங் கலை is sarcasm: the kings who failed at the art of the vina now turn to the sword, and Padumukan blesses their 'learning'. The lion-like king is the bride's father, Kaluzhavegan, whose daughter they could not win by his rule.

750.reading: An elephant whose three musths put other elephants to flight changes its anger once it takes a ball of sweet food; let them think again, for she cannot be released to anyone: the honey-dripping garlanded lady is such a one to the Nambi, Padumukan says.
750.nuance: The comparison is hard: அதிங்கம் is a sweet root, and the point may be that Civakan, like a tamed bull elephant, is settled with his portion, or that she is to him what that morsel is to the elephant. The reading follows the last two lines, which are clear.

751.reading: When a bull stands embracing a young heifer among the herd, do the other bulls, thinking of their strength, strive with him? If the girl of jasmine-bud teeth stands embracing Civakan, can they unite with her except by rising up in anguish to seize her?
751.nuance: The first of three animal proofs (751 to 753): bull and heifer, lion and lioness, musth elephant and cow-elephant. Each gives a law of the herd that the kings, as men, are breaking.

752.reading: When a lion that springs into the sky has mounted its lioness, can even a fierce tiger leap on it? If Prince Civakan has embraced the carp-eyed one, ghouls, is it possible even for the bodiless Love god to go and approach her?
752.nuance: பேய்காள், 'you ghouls', is Padumukan's word for the kings. Not even Anangan, desire itself, could come near her now; still less those whom desire drives.

753.reading: When a musth elephant with the must flowing from its mouth stands by a noble cow-elephant, is a calf fit to attack it? If the chaste doll of a girl belongs to the Nambi Civakan, kings, are they fit to strive for her?

claims.claim: a chaste woman who belongs to one man is beyond the reach of any other

753.nuance: பத்தினிப் பாவை: the word for the chaste wife is used of a bride on the day she garlands her husband. Her karpu begins with the choice, not with years of marriage, and it is said to make her unreachable by force.

754.reading: Not even Indra, whose chest bears a heavenly garland, could part the smoke-scented garlanded lady from the companion of her shoulders; listen further, you who are ruined: can those who burn with desire, thinking to unite with Rati, part her from Kama?
754.nuance: The pair is Kama and Rati: to want this bride is to want Rati away from Kama. The comparison makes the kings' lust its own refutation.

755.reading: Even if they defeat us, Padumukan says, the king who stays behind after their victory will divide them, and when they have fought among themselves and perished he will rule a world made cruel; that is the policy he is breeding, and that is his mind, which they do not see.
755.nuance: இருந்த வேந்தன், the king who sat by, is Kattiyankaran, who urged the fight but did not join it. Padumukan answers his incitement (742 to 745) with its motive: a usurper's policy of letting rival kings destroy one another. நீதி here names a ruler's craft, not justice.

756.reading: Not mere strength of words, kings: gather and see the strength of our bows, he says, and fitting a fierce arrow to the bow and drawing it, he shoots it through a mass of stone so that it hides itself in the earth, saying 'such is our people's learning', like a thunderbolt.
756.event: Padumukan shoots an arrow through a rock into the ground to show the kings his side's skill at arms.
756.nuance: The answer to the taunt of cowardice is a display, not a blow: the arrow goes into the earth. கல்வி here is skill at arms, so the chapter's 'learning' runs from the vina to the bow.

links.note: The Kural says tapas is striven for here because one gets what one wants as one wants it; the bride's falling garland is read as a call to all the world to do tapas.
links.teaches: The Cintamani takes the Kural's frankly worldly motive for tapas and fixes it on a bridal union, showing how far that motive reaches in a work whose hero will at last renounce such joys.

gains.a: the poet's fancy gains a rule that makes it more than a compliment: the joy is the earned fruit of former tapas
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed 'what is wanted' is given a concrete object, sensual and married, which the next couplet's condemnation of desire leaves out

links.note: Kattiyankaran tells cowardly kings to leave their crowns and go to the hermits' forest; the patikam says Civakan renounced at the height of his rule.
links.teaches: In the villain's mouth giving up the crown for the forest is the punishment of a beaten king, while the epic's own ending makes it the free act of a victorious one, so the book stages the courtly contempt for renunciation it will overturn.

links.note: Dharmadattan warned Kattiyankaran that a king is a fire that burns whoever touches him; Padumukan warns the kings that fire burns when touched.
links.teaches: The fire that was said to guard the true king now guards his unknown son against the same usurper's tools, so the proverb points at Civakan's royal birth before anyone in the hall knows it.

links.note: The astrologer read that the princess's destined husband lives in Rajamapuram; Padumukan declares her the chaste bride of Civakan whom no one can take.
links.teaches: What the horoscope fixed as her allotted portion becomes, once she has chosen, her own karpu, so the fated union is defended in the hall as a matter of the woman's chastity rather than of the stars.

links.note: Kattiyankaran promises the kings fortune if they kill Civakan; Padumukan says his plan is to let them destroy one another and rule alone.
links.teaches: Padumukan's reading turns the promise of sovereignty into its opposite, showing the reader that the usurper's incitement of the suitors repeats the method by which he took Saccandan's throne.

links.note: The Kural counts dividing others among a minister's skills; Padumukan exposes the minister-turned-king's plan to divide the kings so they perish fighting each other.
links.teaches: The craft of division that the Kural lists without moral comment as a minister's skill is shown here in the hands of a minister who betrayed his king, and the epic names its result as a world made cruel.

gains.a: Padumukan's charge gains a recognised name: Kattiyankaran is practising the minister's art of division, not mere spite
gains.b: the couplet's neutral skill gains a case where it is turned against the realm, which the couplet does not consider

links.note: In the Purananuru poem a king's demand for a girl her father will not give brings war on the town, and the mother who reared her beauty is blamed; here kings rise to seize a bride already won in an open contest.
links.teaches: The epic removes the father's refusal that drives the Sangam bride-war, since the bride's father set a fair contest and she has chosen, so the suitors' war stands as bare lust and the blame moves from the girl's rearing to the kings and their instigator.

gains.a: the scene is placed in the old category of the bride-war (மகட்பால்), which shows what it changes
gains.b: the poem's blame of the mother is shown to be one choice of cause, which a later poet assigns instead to the suitors' desire and to a schemer

links.note: The Kural asks what a sword is to those without courage and what learning is to those who fear the assembly; Padumukan mocks kings who lost at the art and turn to the sword.
links.teaches: The Kural tests the sword and learning separately, each by its own courage, but Padumukan adds that one who has failed the test of art cannot seek the same prize by the sword, so the second arena only confirms the first defeat.

gains.a: the sarcasm வாழ்க நுங் கலை gains a standard: the kings fail both of the Kural's tests at once
gains.b: the couplet's paired measures gain a rule of contest about moving from one to the other, which the couplet does not state

new_concepts.gloss: the chaste wife whose steadfastness gives her word power over kings, cities and nature
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: பத்தினிப் பாவை (753)

source_issues: 743: the lines appear out of order; line 2 ends with என்றான் and lines 3-4 read as the verse's opening (sense taken as 3, 4, 1, 2).
741 line 3 (கள்ளராற் புலியை யேறு காணிய) is obscure; the comparison cannot be fixed.
745 lines 1-2 and 750 lines 1-2 are hard to construe; readings follow the clear closing lines.
734 lines 1-2 and 744 line 1 carry repaired TSCII slips (ோ் read as ேர்); the repairs read correctly.
